# Intro: what are R and RStudio? {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

No programming experience needed

## What is R?

R is a **language for working with data**. You write short instructions; R carries them out.

```{r}
#| eval: false
mean(c(12, 15, 9))   # "give me the average of 12, 15 and 9"
```

<br>

::: {.incremental}
- In a spreadsheet you **click** to get a result, and the clicks are gone.
- In R you **write down** each step. The steps are saved, so you can rerun, check or share them.
- That written list of steps is a **script**. Writing one is all the "programming" you will do today.
:::

## R and RStudio are two different things

::: {.duo}
::: {}
[R]{.big}
The **engine**. It does the calculations. You rarely open it directly.
:::
::: {.accent}
[RStudio]{.big}
The **dashboard**. A program for writing, running and organizing R code, with panes for your data, plots and help.
:::
:::

<br>

You install both, but you only ever open **RStudio**. It runs R for you behind the scenes.

::: notes
Car analogy: R is the engine, RStudio is the dashboard and steering wheel. Both are free. RStudio is made by a company called Posit.
:::

## You already do this in a spreadsheet

| What you want | Spreadsheet | R |
|---|---|---|
| Average a column | `=AVERAGE(B2:B345)` | `mean(body_mass_g)` |
| Keep some rows | Filter menu, tick boxes | `filter(species == "Gentoo")` |
| Sort | Sort button | `arrange(body_mass_g)` |
| Make a chart | Chart wizard | `ggplot(...)` |
| Redo it all on new data | Repeat every click | **Rerun the script** |

<br>

If you've written a spreadsheet formula, you've already written code.

## Why R?

::: {.incremental}
- **Reproducible.** Your analysis is a script. Rerun it and get the same answer, or point it at new data.
- **Free and open.** No licence, runs on every OS, used across every research field.
- **Huge ecosystem.** 20,000+ packages on CRAN for statistics, figures, text, maps, surveys, genomics.
- **A record of what you did.** Reviewers, collaborators and future-you can see every step.
:::

::: notes
Ask the room: who uses Excel, SPSS, Stata, Prism? Frame R as the same work, written down.
:::

## What to expect today

- **It will feel slower than clicking at first.** The payoff comes the second time you run an analysis.
- **Errors are normal**, even for experts. Each one tells you what to fix, and we'll practise reading them.
- **Type along** rather than copy-paste. Your fingers learn the syntax.
- **Ask anytime.** If you're stuck, someone else is too.

# Warm-up: variables and functions {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

Two ideas you already know, from math and from everyday life

## Quick check

In math class you saw:

$$y = 2x + 3$$

::: {.incremental}
- What is **x**?
- If x = 4, what is **y**?
- What is the **rule** that turns x into y?
:::

::: notes
Ask for answers from the room. x is a variable (a name for a number); y = 11; the rule "double it and add 3" is a function. Everything in R is built from these two ideas.
:::

## Variables: a name that stands for a value

| | Example | The name | The value |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Math** | x = 5, so x + 2 = 7 | `x` | 5 |
| **Everyday** | A contact in your phone called "Mom" | Mom | her phone number |
| **R** | `x <- 5`, then `x + 2` gives 7 | `x` | 5 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,46,20,20]"}

<br>

::: {.incremental}
- You use the **name**; R looks up the **value**.
- In R a variable is called an **object**, and `<-` means "store this value under this name".
- Unlike in math, the value can be **replaced**: `x <- 10` puts a new number under the same name, like updating Mom's number.
:::

## Functions: input → rule → output

| | Example | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Math** | f(x) = 2x + 3, so f(4) | 4 | 11 |
| **Everyday** | A coffee machine | beans, water, "large" | a large coffee |
| **R** | `round(3.14159, digits = 2)` | 3.14159 and 2 | 3.14 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,46,20,20]"}

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="box">3.14159, 2<span class="lbl">inputs</span></div>
  <div class="arrow">→</div>
  <div class="box fn">round()<span class="lbl">function</span></div>
  <div class="arrow">→</div>
  <div class="box">3.14<span class="lbl">output</span></div>
</div>
```

In R: **name of the function**, then inputs in round brackets. The inputs are called **arguments**.

## Knowledge check [3 min]{.timer}

::: {.exercise}
1. In `height <- 172`, what is the name and what is the value?
2. In `sqrt(16)`, what is the function, the input, and the output?
3. After `price <- 4` and then `price <- price + 1`, what is `price`?
:::

. . .

1. Name `height`, value 172
2. Function `sqrt` (square root), input 16, output 4
3. **5**. Read it as "take the old price, add 1, store it back as price". In math, x = x + 1 is impossible; in R, `<-` means *store*, not *equals*.

# Part 1: Setup and RStudio {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

20 minutes

## Install R, then RStudio

1. **R** from [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/): the engine
2. **RStudio Desktop** from [posit.co](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/): the dashboard

<br>

Then open **RStudio** (not R).

::: notes
Common snag: Windows users without admin rights. Anyone who installed beforehand can explore the RStudio window while others catch up.
:::

## The four panes

::: {.panes}
::: {.pane .main}
**Source**
Scripts you save. Your analysis lives here.
:::
::: {.pane}
**Environment**
Objects currently in memory.
:::
::: {.pane}
**Console**
Runs code immediately. Quick checks only.
:::
::: {.pane}
**Files · Plots · Packages · Help**
File browser, figures, installed packages, documentation.
:::
:::


Run a line from a script: **Ctrl+Enter** (Windows) · **Cmd+Enter** (Mac)

## Install the packages

**Packages** are free add-ons that give R extra tools, like apps on a phone.
Install the ones we need by typing this into the **Console** and pressing Enter:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "palmerpenguins", "here",
                   "broom", "car", "emmeans", "janitor", "Hmisc",
                   "patchwork", "quarto", "renv"))
```

<br>

Text will scroll by for a few minutes. That's normal. Red text isn't always an error; look for the word **Error**.

::: notes
Installs take 3–5 minutes. Start them now and move on to Projects while they run. macOS users may need Xcode command line tools for some packages.
:::

## Your workspace

Everything you work with in an analysis lives in one of two places:

::: {.duo}
::: {.accent}
[Files]{.big}
Saved on your computer, in a folder: your data, your scripts, your figures.
**Permanent.** Still there tomorrow.
:::
::: {}
[Memory]{.big}
The objects you create while working, listed in the **Environment** pane.
**Temporary.** Gone when you close or restart R.
:::
:::

<br>

Keep all the files for one analysis in **one folder**. R then knows where to find them, and nothing gets lost on your Desktop or in Downloads.

::: notes
Ask: where do your data files live right now? Most people will say Desktop, Downloads, or email attachments. That's the problem a project folder solves. We come back to the Memory side in Part 2.
:::

## The working directory

R is always "standing in" one folder: the **working directory**.
When you name a file, R looks for it there.

```{r}
#| eval: false
getwd()                    # "get working directory": where is R standing?
#> "/Users/you/Documents"

read_csv("penguins.csv")   # looks for /Users/you/Documents/penguins.csv
#> Error: 'penguins.csv' does not exist in current working directory
#> ('/Users/you/Documents').
```

::: {.live}
→ Type `getwd()` in your Console. Where is R standing?
:::

::: notes
The Files pane shows the same folder. Most people will see their home or Documents folder. That error message is one of the most common beginner errors; now they know what it means.
:::

## Two kinds of file path

| Path | Example | Like… | Works on |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Absolute**: the full address | `"/Users/you/Desktop/project/data/penguins.csv"` | A full street address | Only your computer |
| **Relative**: starts from the working directory | `"data/penguins.csv"` | "Second door on the left" | Any computer, if R is standing in the right folder |

<br>

Relative paths are portable, but only if R starts in the right folder. So how do we set it?

## Setting the working directory

Three ways, from least to most reproducible:

1. **In code:** `setwd("/Users/you/Desktop/project")`
2. **From the menu:** Session → Set Working Directory → Choose Directory…
3. **Open an RStudio Project:** the working directory is set to the project folder automatically ✓

<br>

Options 1 and 2 work today, on your computer. Option 3 works on anyone's computer, every time.

::: notes
Option 2 leaves no record in the script, so a collaborator won't know where you were standing. Option 1 records it, but with an address that only exists on your machine (next slides).
:::

## One RStudio Project per analysis

An **RStudio Project** is one folder for one analysis. Opening it sets the working directory to that folder, so relative paths just work.

File → New Project → New Directory

```
penguin-analysis/
├── penguin-analysis.Rproj   # double-click to open the project
├── data/
│   ├── raw/          # never edited
│   └── processed/    # written by your scripts
├── R/                # analysis scripts
├── figures/
└── report.qmd
```

::: {.live}
→ Switch to RStudio: create this project together, then run `getwd()` again
:::

## Why not just use `setwd()`?

Your script, run on a collaborator's laptop:

```{r}
#| eval: false
setwd("C:/Users/me/Desktop/project")
#> Error in setwd("C:/Users/me/Desktop/project"): cannot change working directory
```

<br>

- That folder doesn't exist on their computer.
- It breaks for **you** too if you rename the folder, move it, or get a new laptop.
- With a Project, there's nothing to set: whoever opens the `.Rproj` starts in the right place.

## `here()`: paths from the project folder

`here()` builds a path starting from the project folder, wherever your script sits inside it.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(here)
here("data", "raw", "penguins_raw.csv")
#> "/Users/you/penguin-analysis/data/raw/penguins_raw.csv"
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Do]{.good}

```r
# open penguin-analysis.Rproj, then:
read_csv(here("data", "raw", "file.csv"))
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Don't]{.bad}

```r
setwd("C:/Users/me/Desktop/project")
read_csv("file.csv")
```
:::
::::

::: {.small .muted}
Why `here()` and not just `"data/raw/file.csv"`? Quarto reports and scripts in subfolders can start in a different folder. `here()` always starts at the project.
:::

# Part 2: R fundamentals {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

40 minutes

## Objects and assignment

Remember variables from the warm-up? In R they're **objects**, created with `<-` (shortcut: **Alt + –**).

```{r}
mass_g <- 3750
species <- "Adelie"
mass_kg <- mass_g / 1000
mass_kg
```

::: {.live}
→ Switch to RStudio: open a new script (File → New File → R Script)
:::

## Vectors: R's basic unit

A vector holds values of one type. Operations apply to **every element at once**.

```{r}
masses <- c(3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450)
masses / 1000
masses[2]               # the 2nd value: counting starts at 1
masses[c(1, 3)]         # the 1st and 3rd values
```

## Data types you'll meet

| Type | Example | Research use |
|---|---|---|
| numeric | `3.75` | Measurements, scores |
| integer | `12L` | Counts |
| character | `"Biscoe"` | Labels, IDs, free text |
| logical | `TRUE`, `FALSE` | Conditions, filters |
| factor | `factor(c("low", "high"))` | Groups, treatments |
| Date | `as.Date("2026-11-15")` | Collection dates |

Check any object with `class(x)`.

## Factors: categories with an order

```{r}
dose <- factor(c("high", "low", "medium", "low"))
levels(dose)            # alphabetical by default

dose <- factor(dose, levels = c("low", "medium", "high"))
levels(dose)            # now in a meaningful order
```

<br>

The **first level is the reference group** in statistical models, and sets the order in plots. Set it on purpose.

## Missing values: `NA`

R won't silently drop data.

```{r}
mean(masses)
mean(masses, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(is.na(masses))
```

<br>

Always report how many observations you dropped, and why.

## Conditions: yes-or-no questions

A **condition** asks a question. R answers `TRUE` or `FALSE`, once for every value.

| | Example |
|---|---|
| **Everyday** | "Which days this week were warmer than 24 °C?" |
| **Spreadsheet** | Filter → Number filters → Greater than… |
| **R** | `temps > 24` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

```{r}
temps <- c(18, 25, 31, 22, 29)   # daily highs, °C
temps > 24
```

## Asking questions in R

| Operator | Question | Example | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `>` `<` | greater / less than? | `5 > 3` | `TRUE` |
| `>=` `<=` | at least / at most? | `5 <= 3` | `FALSE` |
| `==` | equal to? | `"Adelie" == "Gentoo"` | `FALSE` |
| `!=` | not equal to? | `"Adelie" != "Gentoo"` | `TRUE` |
| `&` | both true? | `temps > 20 & temps < 30` | per value |
| `|` | either true? | `temps < 20 | temps > 30` | per value |

<br>

Watch out: `==` **asks** "is it equal?". `<-` **stores** a value. Mixing them up is the most common beginner slip.

## Using conditions

```{r}
temps[temps > 24]                # keep the values where the answer is TRUE
sum(temps > 24)                  # TRUE counts as 1: how many warm days?
mean(temps > 24)                 # share of days that were warm
```

. . .

A missing value gives a missing answer, so tell R what to do with it:

```{r}
masses > 3500
sum(masses > 3500, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: notes
Pt. 2's filter() is this same idea applied to rows of a table: filter(penguins, body_mass_g > 3500).
:::

## Functions and packages

From the warm-up: a function takes inputs (**arguments**) and returns an output.

```{r}
round(3.14159, digits = 2)
```

A package bundles functions.

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("palmerpenguins")   # once per computer
library(palmerpenguins)              # once per session
```

## Getting help

- `?mean`: help page; scroll to **Examples** at the bottom
- `??regression`: search every installed help page
- Read errors **from the end**: the last line names the problem
- Asking others? Make a minimal example with the `reprex` package

```{r}
#| eval: false
?mean
```

## Where does your work live? [5 min]{.timer}

::: {.exercise}
1. Save your script: **Ctrl+S** / **Cmd+S**.
2. Look at the Environment pane. Every object you made is listed.
3. Restart R: **Session → Restart R**. What happened to the Environment?
4. Rerun your whole script: **Ctrl+Shift+Enter** / **Cmd+Shift+Enter**.
:::

. . .

Everything came back. **Your script is your backup, not what's in memory.**

- Objects in memory are temporary; the steps in your script rebuild them.
- Protect the script: save often, and keep the project in a backed-up folder (OneDrive, Google Drive, Dropbox). Pt. 2 adds version control.

::: notes
Let them discover it. Before step 4 ask: "If you hadn't saved the script, what would you have lost?" The answer they reach is the point of the slide.
:::

## Optional: start every session clean

When you quit, RStudio asks **"Save workspace image?"** That's the **Memory** side of your workspace: the objects, not the steps that made them.

Many R users turn it off so nothing works only because of leftovers in memory:

Tools → Global Options → General

- **Restore .RData into workspace at startup:** unchecked
- **Save workspace to .RData on exit:** Never

::: {.small .muted}
Your choice. If you leave it on, restart R and rerun your script before you trust a result.
:::

## Exercise: vectors [5 min]{.timer}

::: {.exercise}
1. Create a vector of five bill lengths (mm), one of them `NA`.
2. Compute the mean, ignoring the missing value.
3. Count how many values are above 40 mm.
:::

. . .

```{r}
bills <- c(39.1, 39.5, NA, 46.5, 50.0)
mean(bills, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(bills > 40, na.rm = TRUE)
```

# Part 3: Importing and inspecting data {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

25 minutes

## Meet the penguins

Our practice data, from the `palmerpenguins` package:

- **344 penguins**, 3 species: Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo
- Collected on 3 islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica, 2007–2009
- One row per penguin: bill length and depth, flipper length, body mass, sex, island, year
- Two versions: `penguins` (cleaned) and `penguins_raw` (as recorded in the field, messy column names)

::: notes
Data collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research program. Ask: what would the equivalent be in your own field?
:::

## Read a CSV

Inside your project, save the raw data, then read it back like a real file:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(here)

dir.create(here("data", "raw"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(penguins_raw, here("data", "raw", "penguins_raw.csv"))

penguins_raw <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "penguins_raw.csv"))
```

<br>

`read_csv()` reports the type it guessed for each column. **Read that message.**
A number column read as text usually means a stray `"n/a"` or `"<0.1"`.

::: notes
Pt. 2 starts from this file, so make sure everyone has it before they leave.
:::

## First look: `glimpse()`

```{r}
glimpse(penguins, width = 70)
```

## First look: `summary()` and `count()`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
summary(penguins$body_mass_g)
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
count(penguins, island)
```
:::
::::

Also try `head(penguins)` and `View(penguins)`.

## Other formats

| Source | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| CSV | `read_csv()` | readr |
| Tab-delimited / instrument output | `read_tsv()`, `read_delim()` | readr |
| Excel | `read_excel(path, sheet = 2)` | readxl |
| SPSS, Stata, SAS | `read_sav()`, `read_dta()`, `read_sas()` | haven |

<br>

Tell R which codes mean missing:
`read_csv(path, na = c("", "NA", "n/a", "-999"))`

## Tidy data

Each **variable** is a column · each **observation** is a row · each **value** is a cell.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Wide: "week" is hidden in the column names]{.bad}

```{r}
#| echo: false
wide <- data.frame(id = 1:2, week1 = c(5.1, 4.8), week2 = c(5.6, 5.0))
print(wide, row.names = FALSE)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Tidy: one row per measurement]{.good}

```{r}
#| echo: false
long <- as.data.frame(pivot_longer(wide, -id, names_to = "week", values_to = "score"))
print(long, row.names = FALSE)
```
:::
::::

::: {.small .muted}
Pt. 2 shows how to reshape with `pivot_longer()`.
:::

## Exercise: inspect the penguins [5 min]{.timer}

::: {.exercise}
1. How many penguins have no recorded sex?
2. Which island has the most penguins?
3. What type is the `year` column?
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| include: false
top_island <- count(penguins, island, sort = TRUE)[1, ]
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
sum(is.na(penguins$sex))
count(penguins, island, sort = TRUE)
class(penguins$year)
```
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
1. **`r sum(is.na(penguins$sex))`** penguins
2. **`r top_island$island`** (`r top_island$n` penguins)
3. **`r class(penguins$year)`**: whole numbers
:::
::::

# Put it together: explore the penguins {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

15 minutes · run the code, then change it

## 1. Who lives where? [5 min]{.timer}

::: {.exercise}
You know `count()` from Part 3. Count penguins by **island and species** together.
Which species live on only one island?
:::

. . .

```{r}
count(penguins, island, species)
```

Gentoo live only on Biscoe and Chinstrap only on Dream; Adelie live on all three islands.

## 2. Averages per group [5 min]{.timer}

::: {.exercise}
Run this, then change it to give the mean **flipper length** per species.
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
```

::: {.small .muted}
Read `|>` as "and then". Pt. 2 explains each piece.
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_flipper_mm =
    mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
```

## 3. Your first plot [5 min]{.timer}

::: {.exercise}
Run this, then put **bill length** on the x-axis. Do the species still separate?
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point()
```

. . .

```{r}
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(penguins,
       aes(x = bill_length_mm,
           y = body_mass_g,
           colour = species)) +
  geom_point()
```

## What you just did

::: {.incremental}
- A few lines replaced a pivot table, a chart wizard, and notes on how you made them.
- Get new data next year? **Rerun the script.** Every number and figure updates.
- Pt. 2 teaches each piece so you can write these from scratch.
:::

# Wrap-up {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

## Ready for Pt. 2?

- ☐ R and RStudio installed; every package installed without errors
- ☐ Your script is saved in the project and reruns cleanly after **Session → Restart R**
- ☐ An RStudio Project with `data/`, `R/` and `figures/`
- ☐ `data/raw/penguins_raw.csv` exists inside it
- ☐ `glimpse(penguins)` runs, and you can name each column's type

<br>

Package won't install? Show the instructor before you leave.

## Errors you'll see this week

| Message | Fix |
|---|---|
| `could not find function "ggplot"` | `library(tidyverse)` |
| `there is no package called 'x'` | `install.packages("x")` |
| `object 'x' not found` | Check spelling and case; run the script from the top |
| `cannot open file ... No such file` | Open the `.Rproj`; build paths with `here()` |
| A `+` in the Console that won't go away | Press **Esc**, fix the line |

## Next time and resources

**Pt. 2:** wrangling with dplyr · figures with ggplot2 · t-tests, ANOVA, regression · Quarto reports

- [R for Data Science (2e)](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/): free, the standard next step
